items.title: Democracies Need Creative Destruction
items.author: Jennifer Pahlka & Andrew Greenway
items.blurb: Argues that dissatisfaction with democracy is partly a delivery problem: governments accumulate procedures they never retire, as when US pandemic surveillance spending failed to detect COVID for a month because labs could not get permission to test swabs.

items.title: The end of an era for China's economy
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Smith argues the growth formula Zhu Rongji built in the 1990s has stopped working for China, and that Xi Jinping's replacement is not obviously going to work either.

items.title: The world's most influential economist is oddly unconvincing
items.blurb: A skeptical assessment of Daron Acemoglu, asking why the most revered living economist of institutions and growth commands the reverence he does.

items.title: Donald Trump's deregulatory drive will cause another financial crisis
items.author: Martin Gruenberg
items.blurb: Gruenberg argues the current rollback of bank rules repeats earlier deregulatory cycles, with the added danger that the institutions meant to contain the damage are themselves weaker this time.

items.title: Why AI systems are most useful as designers of new scientific tools
items.author: James Evans
items.blurb: Reviewing Alexander Krauss's The Engine of Scientific Discovery, Evans argues that because breakthroughs historically follow new instruments, AI's largest contribution to science may be designing the next generation of them rather than producing findings itself.

items.title: Universities must stop protecting bullies — or more people will leave science
items.author: Morteza Mahmoudi
items.blurb: After collecting several thousand case reports through the Academic Parity Movement, Mahmoudi finds universities failing in both directions — letting powerful academics off the hook while increasingly overreacting to allegations — and says the people who leave are the cost.

items.title: AI and the New Age of Bioweapons
items.author: Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall
items.blurb: Sherwood-Randall's scenario is a low-skill group using a jailbroken model trained on comprehensive biological data to design a more lethal H5N1 strain, and she argues biosecurity policy is not built for the convergence of AI with bioengineering.

items.title: OpenAI funds research to try to stop AI from being used to make bioweapons
items.blurb: OpenAI is granting money to the Nuclear Threat Initiative to build an international information-sharing system for flagging biosecurity threats that originate with AI models.

items.title: NSF announces $1.5B for foundational research to drive scientific breakthroughs
items.blurb: Twelve new funding notices worth over $1.5 billion move NSF toward portfolio-based grantmaking, mixing long-horizon awards with rapid short-term grants meant to test ideas quickly and cut administrative burden.

items.title: AI hasn't gone rogue. It's worse than that
items.blurb: The recent cyber attacks did not involve models escaping their instructions; they show models doing what they were trained to do while the safeguards around them fall short.

items.title: Africa Can't Afford to Squander Its Demographic Opportunity
items.author: Jakkie Cilliers
items.blurb: Cilliers argues that the age structure of a population, more than corruption or weak institutions, is the strongest single predictor of growth, stability, and democratic consolidation across African countries.

items.title: How China Found Its Most Potent Weapon
items.author: Gloria Xiong & Jessica Chen Weiss
items.blurb: Deng Xiaoping's 1992 line that China has rare earths as the Middle East has oil is now read in Washington as a decades-old coercive plan; the authors reconstruct how the dominance was actually built.

items.title: The Cost of Keeping China Out
items.author: Peter Cowhey & Meg Rithmire
items.blurb: A technology-policy scholar and a political economist argue that blanket American suspicion of Chinese investment costs the United States more in competitiveness than it gains in security.

items.title: America's Missing Military Revolution
items.author: Doug Beck
items.blurb: Beck's analogy for defense procurement is buying a phone you must test for three years, cannot upgrade, and receive two years later — the reason, he argues, Washington keeps losing ground in the technology race.

items.title: China's exorbitant surplus calls for a much stronger yuan
items.author: Brad Setser
items.blurb: Setser argues that appreciating the yuan would do more than tariffs to address global concern about China's reliance on exports for growth.

items.author: Jake Currie

items.title: Some fertility and AI forecasts
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen flags a new fertility projection on which global GDP in 2100 is 10 percent lower, payroll taxes to fund old-age benefits are far higher, and China's share of world output falls from 25.6 to 14.9 percent while America's rises from 11.2 to 14.4 percent.

items.title: NIH proposes major revamp of how it scores research grant proposals
items.author: Max Kozlov
items.blurb: For five decades the NIH reported the exact numerical peer-review score of each proposal; the new plan reports only a top, middle or bottom tier, which proponents call an honest admission that three reviewers cannot support that precision and critics call cover for political interference.

items.title: What Really Happens If China Wins the AI Race?
items.author: Matteo Wong
items.blurb: The tech industry has portrayed Chinese AI development as an existential threat for years; Wong argues what would actually follow from Chinese models leading is less straightforward than that framing implies.

items.title: Daycare pseudoscience
items.author: Phoebe Arslanagic-Little
items.blurb: Both the claim that daycare traumatizes toddlers and the claim that it lays the foundation for later success are made with confidence the evidence does not support: whether a child attends daycare usually makes little difference to their outcomes.

items.title: Treat biological databases as infrastructure, not projects
items.author: Neil Hall et al.
items.blurb: PomBase, the knowledge hub for fission yeast, has lost its long-term Wellcome support and FlyBase lost the NIH award that paid its curation team in 2025 — the authors argue curated databases are load-bearing for modern biology but funded as time-limited projects.

items.title: The White House's absurd claim of a Chinese transshipment "scam"
items.blurb: Rejects the administration's charge that Chinese goods rerouted through third countries constitute a scam, arguing this is the predictable effect of high tariffs rather than evidence of fraud.

items.title: How economics is changing
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Causal claims rose from 7.7 percent of claims in the economics literature in 1990 to 32.6 percent in 2023, and papers making more of them are likelier to be cited and to land in the top five journals, while econometric theory and monetary policy shrink as a share of output.

items.title: The invisible faction that dominates the Democratic Party
items.author: Matthew Yglesias
items.blurb: Yglesias argues the standard reading of this summer's primaries as left-wing insurgents against a moderate establishment collapses two different strands of progressivism, and that the strand which actually sets party positions is rarely on the ballot.

items.title: Scientists cited by Heritage Foundation report on women's sports say it misrepresented their research
items.blurb: The think tank's report claims that high-intensity and elite sports training leaves lasting effects on menstrual cycles and fertility; the researchers it cites say that is not what their work found.
